title: RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI)
gist: Rust co-lead designer and Amazon Senior Principal Engineer Niko Matsakis argues AI agents erase Rust's learning-curve barrier while AI-driven vulnerability discovery and cheap million-line rewrites push the industry toward memory-safe, statically verifiable languages. He presents Symposium (an agent-oriented Rust toolchain letting crate authors ship skills/MCP/hooks) and the Agent Client Protocol as fixes for poorly extensible, non-portable vertical coding agents.

themes.theme: Why AI makes Rust's adoption curve disappear

insights.claim: Rust lead designer Niko Matsakis argues AI agents remove Rust's main adoption barrier — the months-long learning curve — because the agent already learned Rust in training, letting teams skip straight to benefiting from a type system that acts as guardrails for agent-generated code.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Language choice friction is collapsing; expect accelerating Rust adoption in AI-heavy shops and rising demand for Rust tooling/expertise.
insights.quote: the agent already learned Rust in its training, its reinforcement learning stages and whatnot
insights.locator: Usually it doesn't win over, but that's changed a lot

insights.claim: Matsakis cites OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman as saying Rust is a perfect language for agents because if it compiles it is approximately correct.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Endorsement from a frontier-lab leader signals agent-friendly, statically checked languages gaining mindshare.
insights.quote: Rust is a perfect language for agents, given that if it compiles, it's approximately correct
insights.locator: You don't have to take it from me

insights.claim: Matsakis argues that when coding becomes cheap, technology-stack choice should be driven by the properties you want in the future (reliability, efficiency, security) rather than what your team already knows — a structural shift in how the industry picks languages.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Legacy-language lock-in weakens as a moat; incumbent-language ecosystems (and the vendors tied to them) face migration risk.
insights.quote: if coding is really cheap, then you should pick not based on what you have, not based on what you know, but based on what you want
insights.locator: Where that leaves me is

insights.claim: Rust is the only language besides C (not even C++) allowed in the Linux kernel and is also used in Microsoft's kernel, while remaining usable for application-level software such as the ratatui TUI library.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Rust's span from kernels to apps broadens its addressable footprint versus C/C++ and managed languages.
insights.quote: We are the only language apart from C, not even C++, that's allowed in the Linux kernel, just C and Rust.
insights.locator: Rust + AI

insights.claim: Matsakis notes he now writes more Python, TypeScript and Swift than before because AI removes his learning-curve penalty — the goal is that developers should not need to care which language is used.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: AI lowers switching costs in every direction, not only toward Rust; language ecosystems compete on agent-tooling quality.
insights.quote: the goal is that you shouldn't care what programming language is being used actually
insights.locator: One thing I've noticed is I'm writing a lot more

themes.theme: AI-driven mass rewrites and Amazon's Rust footprint

insights.claim: Rust adoption at Amazon is driven by efficiency at scale: S3, EC2 and Lambda were the first adopters on critical data paths, and the DSQL serverless SQL database team expanded from one narrow part to Rust across data plane, control plane and Postgres bindings.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler cost-per-request economics favor Rust; watch AWS services migrating for compute savings.
insights.locator: I'm only going to use it in the critical data paths

insights.claim: Matsakis says AI-driven rewrites now make it possible to move large codebases in weeks or months that previously took decades or failed, citing a Microsoft research effort targeting a million lines per engineer and Bun's production move of roughly a million lines from Zig to Rust.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Migration cost is no longer a barrier — expect a wave of legacy-to-Rust rewrites and the services/tools that support them.
insights.quote: it's now possible to move large codebases in a matter of weeks or months, which used to take decades or infinity because it usually failed
insights.locator: Of course, then Bun is running off

insights.claim: Matsakis hints that similar AI-driven rewrite experiments are underway at Amazon and many FAANG companies with what he calls surprisingly high rates of success, though he says he cannot confirm details.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Big-tech internal rewrite programs may surface publicly; a leading indicator of Rust demand and agent-assisted migration tooling.
insights.quote: I can neither confirm nor deny that similar experiments are taking place at Amazon and in many FAANG companies
insights.locator: Of course, then Bun is running off

insights.claim: The codex-rs project, which used to be written in TypeScript, is being ported to Rust, which Matsakis cites as an example of Rust's broad applicability pulling projects in.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Agent tooling itself is moving to Rust — signals where agent-infrastructure engineering is heading.
insights.locator: In terms of this range of applications

themes.theme: AI-found vulnerabilities as a forcing function for memory safety

insights.claim: Matsakis argues AI vulnerability-finding (he references Mythos) is a 'doctor's orders' forcing function: code in memory-unsafe languages like C/C++, or languages relying heavily on reflection, will have vulnerabilities found by attackers' AI, pushing teams toward statically verifiable languages.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Security pressure from AI offense is a durable tailwind for memory-safe languages and static verification tools; a headwind for C/C++ codebases.
insights.quote: there's tons of vulnerabilities all scattered throughout your code, and I can help you find them, and I can help your attackers find them, too
insights.locator: There's one other factor, though

insights.claim: Matsakis predicts an accelerating need for high levels of software validation because once software ships — open source or merely reverse-engineerable — someone can run AI against it to find vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Pre-ship verification and secure-by-construction tooling become mandatory spend.
insights.quote: the minute it ships, somebody else can be running an AI against it
insights.locator: I think this is going to be an accelerating trend

insights.claim: The long-cited statistic that roughly 70% of vulnerabilities relate to memory safety was unchanged for 20-plus years despite static checkers like Coverity; Android data shows new memory-safety vulnerabilities track the volume of new memory-unsafe code linearly, so switching to Rust (and Kotlin) actually moves the number.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Language migration, not bolt-on scanners, is what reduces vulnerability counts — challenges the value proposition of static analysis vendors for memory bugs.
insights.quote: Whether you bring in Coverity or all these static checkers and all this other stuff, it's always the same, until now.
insights.locator: This has been a story for a while. Android

insights.claim: Matsakis cites a Linux kernel leader named Greg as saying Rust will save Linux from AI, meaning a systematic fix is needed because continuous patching cannot keep up with AI-discovered vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Linux kernel Rust adoption likely to deepen; continuous-patching approaches lose credibility.
insights.quote: Rust will save Linux from AI
insights.locator: Switching to a new language that actually rules it out

insights.claim: Models lag fast-moving ecosystems: Claude did not know the new Toasty ORM existed, and when told to use it, burned many tokens searching the web and produced code on Toasty 0.3 when 0.5 was current, plus the three-year-old Rust 2021 edition rather than Rust 2024.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Training-data staleness is a structural limit — creates a market for live, authoritative context injection into agents.
insights.quote: The training cycle is this slow-moving average of the web.
insights.locator: When I asked Claude about it

insights.claim: Matsakis complains that as a Rust compiler and language designer he has no influence over what Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or OpenCode do, because these are vertical, not readily extensible applications.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Closed agent products leave an opening for open extensibility layers; ecosystem owners will push for hooks into agents.
insights.quote: These are all these vertical applications that aren't easily and readily extensible.
insights.locator: Another thing I see even with the latest models

insights.claim: Symposium is an open-source, agent-oriented toolchain in the Rust Foundation's Innovation Lab, installed via 'cargo install symposium' and 'cargo agents init', which configures chosen agents to invoke it and injects baseline guidance such as using Rust 2024, cargo add for latest crate versions, and cargo fmt.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Language foundations building agent-facing toolchains is a new pattern; watch adoption as a proxy for agent-native developer tooling.
insights.locator: Symposium + Rust + AI

insights.claim: Symposium lets crate authors ship skills (and MCP servers and hooks) with their crates; it detects a project's dependencies and installs the matching skills locally, so agents get version-accurate guidance instead of searching the web and burning tokens.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Library-author-distributed agent context could become standard across package ecosystems (npm, PyPI) — a distribution channel for dev-tool vendors.
insights.quote: instead of going off to search the web and burn tokens and come up with an old version of Toasty, you would just get the results right there
insights.locator: This is trying to work around that problem

insights.claim: Symposium's 'crate info' API simply hands agents the exact-version crate source from Cargo's cache, which Matsakis finds better than letting agents hallucinate APIs or parse HTML docs, because agents are very good at grepping source.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Cheap, deterministic context beats retrieval from the web — a design principle for token-efficient agent tooling.
insights.quote: They're very good at grepping through source as it happens.
insights.locator: It also has various APIs

insights.claim: Symposium currently requires a centralized 'recommendations' repository entry before pulling a crate's skills, as a practical security compromise because dependency-supplied guidance could instruct agents to do malicious things — a risk Matsakis likens to existing build hooks.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Agent-context supply chain needs trust registries; a nascent security category.
insights.quote: We have to at least say, yes, we trust that crate author or that crate organization not to do something malicious
insights.locator: I mentioned that we are still requiring something in the central repo

themes.theme: Battery packs, profiling and ecosystem funding

insights.claim: Matsakis says the biggest frustration for Rust adopters is not learning the language but navigating the library ecosystem; 'battery packs' are special crates bundling vetted library lists, cross-cutting docs and Symposium extensions for a purpose such as network services.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Curated, opinionated stacks lower adoption friction — whoever curates them gains ecosystem influence.
insights.quote: learning the language isn't usually their biggest problem
insights.locator: How do you know? When I talk to people who are adopting Rust

insights.claim: Matsakis (who works at Amazon) describes work toward an opinionated network-service battery pack that includes a profiler using perf and Linux hardware events correlated with the Rust scheduler and exposed to agents, letting agents diagnose production P99 spikes down to lines of code with what he calls tremendous results.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Agent-readable profiling data is a new observability use case; competes/complements APM vendors.
insights.quote: Rust gives you control, not performance.
insights.locator: We're working towards having an opinionated network service pack

insights.claim: The Rust Foundation is spinning up a Rust commercial network for industrial users to share production library lists, partly to direct funding to open-source maintainers who face growing pressure from AI without effective support mechanisms.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Open-source maintainer burden under AI is a systemic risk; corporate funding mechanisms are emerging.
insights.locator: Opinionated network service, that's great

themes.theme: Agent portability and the Agent Client Protocol

insights.claim: Agent portability is poor: library READMEs carry separate instructions for Claude, Codex and Gemini, even AGENTS.md is not universally honored, and hook events differ in availability and JSON field names across agents, forcing Symposium to write skills into both .agents and .claude directories and define its own hook format.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Fragmentation is a tax on ecosystem builders; standards that abstract agents would capture value.
insights.quote: Even AGENTS.md is not universally supported.
insights.locator: Portability Across Agents

insights.claim: The Agent Client Protocol (ACP), originally created so the Zed editor could support many agents via JSON-RPC, now has broad adoption: an agent registry (with wrappers for some, like Claude, written unofficially), IntelliJ-family IDEs, Emacs, Neovim, Obsidian, TUIs like Toad and Nori, and OpenClaw.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: ACP decouples agent from frontend — commoditizes agent UIs and lowers switching costs between model vendors.
insights.locator: Agent Client Protocol (ACP)

insights.claim: Matsakis argues newer agents adopt ACP natively as a foothold strategy, since supporting it gives them instant access to every ACP client and spares them from building their own GUI.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Open protocols favor challengers over incumbents with proprietary UIs; watch which leading agents adopt natively.
insights.locator: A classic problem. They created this protocol

insights.claim: Matsakis's vision of 'agent mods' — ACP middleware sitting between client and agent that can rewrite prompts, augment context, inject tools and fork sub-agents — would give extensions control that skills, MCP servers and hooks lack.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: An agent middleware layer could become a new platform/control point, analogous to editor extension ecosystems.
insights.quote: It's still like an unstable part of the spec, but it's like middleware.
insights.locator: This gets us to the latest thing

insights.claim: Matsakis expects agentic coding standards to be needed for complex workflows, noting strong enterprise interest in building agent integrations for employees that go beyond a CLI.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Enterprise internal agent platforms built on open protocols is a demand signal for integration vendors.
insights.locator: As agentic coding becomes more mainstream

insights.claim: Matsakis's retcon git-history tool worked about 90% of the time as a pure LLM script but often skipped branches or tests; rewriting it with a deterministic Rust backing over ACP guarantees every commit passes tests and is formatted — he argues deterministic scaffolding plus telemetry on skill usage is needed rather than prompt nudges.
insights.speaker: Niko Matsakis
insights.so_what: Deterministic orchestration around LLMs beats prompt-only skills for reliability; telemetry/A-B tooling for agent skills is an unmet need.
insights.quote: I feel we need deterministic stuff, and I feel we need a way to measure, are we actually helping or not?
insights.locator: How do we nudge the LLM to be more deterministic?
